drafts.raw_submission: We the people demand end to end transparency for all govt. funded contracts... we need the private organizations finances as related to the government contracts... that's the end game for the only true transparency of knowing where every dollar lands.
drafts.neutral_framing: Should Clark County require end-to-end public reporting — who received the money, what it bought, and what it achieved — as a written condition of every contract, grant, and incentive the county funds?
drafts.final_wording: Should Clark County require public reporting of who was paid, how much, and for what, for every contract, grant and incentive it funds?
drafts.final_wording_note: Wording made neutral in October 2026: opinions on this site live only in petitions. Earlier wording is in the repository history.
shaping_notes: The neutral framing converts a demand into a yes/no question an official body could actually act on, per the charter. The submitter chooses the final wording; both versions are logged per the Idea Shaper ownership rules.

A county cannot open a private company’s books. It can set conditions on its own money, such as disclosure clauses in contracts and incentive agreements. The question is framed around what the county can require.

The documents behind this question are on this site: $1.84M a year in EDCCC incentives with no public recipient list in the documents we hold, commodity purchases no posted document names, and an ambulance contract whose terms are not in a public document we hold. The question is whether the county should require reporting beyond what the law requires.

Pre-vote checklist per the charter: neutrality review, human review against bright lines (no named-individual conduct — this is a policy question, clears), official partner conversation (county judge / quorum court are the actors), and conflict-of-interest disclosure: the platform’s sponsor and founder is a county business owner; that relationship is disclosed on the issue page.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll during the site's quiet launch: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Per the charter, Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.

drafts.neutral_framing: Should Clark County government fund community food-growing programs — gardens on public land, a gleaning and produce-sharing network, and school and campus gardens?
drafts.final_wording: Should Clark County government fund community food-growing programs — gardens on public land, a gleaning and produce-sharing network, and school and campus gardens?
drafts.final_wording_note: Opened by the platform’s founder during the site’s quiet launch. Wording made neutral in October 2026; earlier wording is in the repository history.
shaping_notes: This is a policy question a county body could act on — not a named-individual conduct question and not an active ballot measure. It clears the charter’s bright lines.

A county cannot guarantee anyone’s food, and this question does not claim it can. It asks whether the county should support community food-growing as ongoing infrastructure — land, coordination, and grant-seeking — the parts a county controls.
The sources are cited on the /food page; where a figure comes from a secondary source, the page says so.

drafts.background: About one in five people in Clark County are food insecure: 20% in the 2023 Feeding America Map the Meal Gap estimate, compared with 19% for Arkansas and 14% for the nation (source). Most food assistance is emergency assistance. This question asks whether the county should also support community food-growing. Every Arkansas county has a Cooperative Extension office (University of Arkansas Extension), and the Arkansas Gleaning Project operates in all 75 counties (Arkansas Hunger Relief Alliance). Sources and precedents are on the Food as a utility page.
drafts.disclosure: This question was opened by the platform’s founder. Unlike the contract-transparency question, no sponsor relationship is at stake here; it is disclosed only because the platform names who opens every question.

shaping_notes: A question about how our shared water is treated — not about any person, candidate, or ballot measure. Clears the bright lines.
Grounded in the utility’s own water-quality report and in published measurements of living filters, with their limits stated on the water page.

drafts.background: Arkadelphia’s 2023 water report (document library) lists trihalomethanes (TTHM) at a 54 ppb running average against an 80 ppb limit. The limit applies to the running annual average, and the report lists no TTHM violation. Individual samples ranged up to 85 ppb. The source water is the Ouachita River, which carries natural organic matter. A biological filter is one method for reducing that organic matter before chlorine is added; results vary by site. The evidence and its limits are on the water page.

drafts.background: Jail garden programs exist elsewhere. In Smith County, Texas, people held in the jail run a garden whose produce goes to the East Texas Food Bank (KETK, June 2023). The Garland County, Arkansas, Detention Center is a University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture site that donates produce to Project Hope Food Bank (Garland County). No garden, GED, trade, recovery or reentry program was found documented at the Clark County jail (Docket #18). A RAND meta-analysis of correctional-education studies found 43% lower odds of returning to prison among participants (RAND RR266). The facts, the evidence, and the limits are on the From holding to building page.
